html:
The map's label, in 323 and 300 BCE, for the many small states of north-western and central India just outside the Nanda and then Maurya realm. Some were kingdoms. Others were republics, called gana-sanghas, ruled by assemblies of leading clan members.

Republics had a long history in India. The Vajji league, led by the Licchavis, was famous in the Buddha's time, and the Buddha's own Shakya people were a clan republic. In the Punjab and Sindh, many such states met Alexander the Great in 326 and 325 BCE. King Porus fought him at the Hydaspes, and the Malavas fought him fiercely in the lower Punjab.

Soon after Alexander left, Chandragupta Maurya brought most of these lands into the Maurya Empire. Some republics, such as the Malavas and the Yaudheyas, survived or came back for centuries afterwards.
